source.title: Flat minima generalize for low-rank matrix recovery
source.authors: Li-Jun Ding; D. Drusvyatskiy; Maryam Fazel; Z. Harchaoui

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures Hessian trace as a flatness criterion and evaluates generalization through recovery of ground truth in low-rank recovery problems, including a synthetic shallow neural network. This conceptually tests the flatness/generalization relation, but not the natural-label classification or memorization claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests whether trace-flat solutions recover ground truth across low-rank sensing, matrix completion, robust PCA, covariance estimation and quadratic-activation networks. Its synthetic numerical recovery results and deep sparse recovery results bear on generalization, but do not measure any listed V1–V8 behavior. Cited prior work on neural-network flatness is not treated as a result.
record.test_reason: The study tests ground-truth recovery by solutions selected to minimize Hessian trace. It does not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation measure, its correlation with train–test gaps, or its ranking against other measures in convolutional networks. Its results also do not test V1–V6 or V8.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the main results. Exact-recovery guarantees apply under stated assumptions, with only weak recovery proved for matrix completion. Synthetic flat-solution recovery nearly matches nuclear-norm minimization; deeper sparse factorizations worsen recovery. Appendix A additionally gives a minimax-rate noisy matrix-sensing guarantee and a numerical comparison with nuclear-norm minimization.
record.recipe_differences: The study optimizes a Hessian-trace flatness criterion through a convex relaxation for low-rank recovery, rather than training standard gradient methods on natural-label tasks; its shallow network uses quadratic activations and synthetic teacher-generated data.
record.method_sensitivity: The deep sparse-recovery experiment reports that recovery error degrades as factorization depth increases; numerical flat-solution recovery is evaluated across problem type, dimension, measurement count and rank, with condition-specific values shown only in figures.

fits_no_version.finding: Under stated statistical assumptions, trace-minimizing interpolating solutions exactly recover ground truth in matrix and bilinear sensing, robust PCA, and quadratic-network/covariance settings. Matrix completion has a weak-recovery theorem and empirical evidence of exact recovery.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hessian-trace minimization can select ground-truth-recovering solutions in specified overparameterized low-rank recovery problems.

fits_no_version.finding: Flat solutions are nearly norm-minimal and nearly balanced under suitable conditioning, but these properties generally do not coincide exactly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trace-flatness implies approximate norm minimality and balancedness in specified matrix-factorization settings.

fits_no_version.finding: In the sparse-recovery experiment, trace-flat solutions recover exactly at depth two, while recovery error worsens as depth increases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing factorization depth can impair ground-truth recovery by trace-flat solutions.

record.peer_reviewed: Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA
record.problems: The empirical recovery curves and regularity measures are reported in figures without condition-specific numerical values in the text. The matrix completion theorem gives weak recovery, while the paper's stronger exact-recovery suggestion is empirical. Experiments use synthetic low-rank recovery settings rather than natural-label classification or standard neural-network training recipes.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant result rows were omitted. The theorem statements and analytical recovery guarantees were not converted into additional rows because they are not separately measured numerical outcomes; numerical condition-specific values for Sections 8 and 9 are figure-only and recorded as such.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level random-label test accuracy, and natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width required for interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error across data sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, correlation with train–test gaps, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures within a convolutional family.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized versus randomly selected training examples.

record.verdict_notes: Related flatness results do not establish or refute V7's specific correlational claim. Appendix A's omitted experiment also fits no listed version, so it does not require a missing entry.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test accuracy coexistence.
Test error as network width grows past interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Effects of dropout and weight decay on test error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with train–test gaps in the specified convolutional family.
Effect on test accuracy of removing the most-memorized training examples.

rows.operation_detail: Varied factorization depth in the flat-solution objective and measured relative signal recovery error.
rows.note: The text states exact recovery at k = 2 and that relative error degrades significantly as k increases; the plotted values are not stated.
rows.check: Depth-dependent sparse recovery does not measure a listed version, so partial is inappropriate. The text explicitly reports exact recovery at k = 2 and worsening error with depth. The measurement count is m = 3⌈r log d⌉, not 3dr log d; the extracted footnote has damaged ceiling symbols. Its description of the signal's nonzero count also inconsistently uses k rather than r.
